metadata.scope: e_mali (251 baronies across k_ghana, k_gurma, k_jenne, k_kaabu, k_mali, k_songhay, k_takrur)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_guidimaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Guidimakha (Gidimaxa) is recorded in Soninke oral tradition and later colonial-era ethnography as a Soninke dyamare (chiefdom) in southern Mauritania and western Mali.
b_guidimaka.etymology_analysis: From Soninke Gidimaxa, the indigenous name of a Soninke chiefdom (dyamare) in the upper Senegal River valley and Assaba foothills; often folk-etymologized in Soninke oral tradition as referring to rock/stone or early Soumaré/Kamara founders.

b_diafunu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written Arabic sources as Zāfqū / Zāfūn by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik), and subsequently by al-Idrisi (1154 CE) and Yaqut al-Hamawi (1220 CE).

morphemes.translation: Dia (ancestral town in the Inner Niger Delta)

b_diafunu.etymology_analysis: Soninke Diafunu (Dyahunu), meaning 'people of Dia', referring to a Soninke dyamare centered on the upper Kolinbiné River in western Mali; rendered in medieval Arabic as Zāfūn.

b_karakoro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; documented in 19th–20th century French colonial geography and hydrography as a right-bank tributary of the Senegal River.
b_karakoro.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Karakoro River, an intermittent right-bank tributary of the Senegal River forming part of the Mali–Mauritania border; the name is of local Soninke/Mande origin.

b_nioro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Nioro (Nioro du Sahel) in northwestern Mali is traditionally said to have been founded in the post-medieval period and is documented in 19th-century written records as capital of Kaarta (1818–1854) and of El Hadj Umar Tall's Toucouleur Empire (captured 1855 CE).
b_nioro.etymology_analysis: From Soninke Ñóoró (modern Nioro du Sahel), an oasis trading center in the Kingui region of northwestern Mali that rose to prominence as capital of the Bambara Kingdom of Kaarta and subsequently of the Toucouleur Empire.

b_kingui.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kingui (Kingi, the Pulaar/Soninke regional name for the Diarra/Diawara kingdom centered around Nioro) is recorded in post-medieval Sahelian oral traditions and 19th-century colonial accounts.

morphemes.translation: Kingui (historical region around Diarra and Nioro)

b_kingui.etymology_analysis: Pulaar and Soninke regional designation (Kingi / Kingui) applied to the Soninke Kingdom of Diarra (founded late 11th century CE) in northwestern Mali around Nioro du Sahel.

b_yelimane.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Yélimané appears in 18th–19th century Kaarta Bambara and French colonial records (e.g., captured by a French column in December 1890 CE).
b_yelimane.etymology_analysis: Local Soninke settlement name in the Guidimé/Diafounou region of western Mali, recorded in 19th-century Kaarta and French colonial history.

b_sorma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Sorma (also Soroma) is documented only in modern Malian administrative geography (Kayes Region).
b_sorma.etymology_analysis: Modern Malian local settlement name in the Kayes Region (Bafoulabé/Diéma area), without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sero.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Sero (Sero Diamanou) is documented only in modern Malian administrative geography in the Kayes Region.
b_sero.etymology_analysis: Local Soninke/Khassonké village name in the Kayes Region of western Mali, unattested in medieval written sources.

b_farabugu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Farabougou (Farabugu), a rural settlement in Mali, is documented only in modern colonial and post-colonial administrative records.
b_farabugu.etymology_analysis: Manding/Bambara settlement toponym (Farabougou) combining the common settlement element -bugu ('hamlet/camp') with fara ('rock/stone' or 'lowland marsh').

b_gemukura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Guémoukoura is attested in 19th-century Umarian and French colonial sources (occupied by Bamana forces in 1870 CE and site of the Battle of Guémoukoura in 1872 CE).
b_gemukura.etymology_analysis: Bambara compound meaning 'New Guémou' (Guémou + koura 'new'), referring to the 19th-century fortress south of Kaarta.

b_diara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Diarra (Jaara / Diara), the historic Soninke capital in northwestern Mali founded in the late 11th century CE after the decline of Ghana, is documented in post-medieval Sahelian oral traditions, 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles, and 19th-century European accounts.
b_diara.etymology_analysis: Soninke toponym (Jaara / Diarra / Diara), seat of the Soninke Kingdom of Diarra in northwestern Mali, established as a successor polity following the decline of the Ghana Empire.

b_kaniaga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kaniaga (Khaniaga) appears in post-medieval oral traditions of the Sosso Empire (12th–13th centuries CE) and 19th–20th century historiography.

morphemes.translation: north / northern land (between upper Senegal and Niger bend)

b_kaniaga.etymology_analysis: Soninke and Malinke historical region name (Kaniaga / Khaniaga), derived from a Malinke term meaning 'north', applied to the region north of Manden where the Sosso Empire arose.

b_bakunu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bakounou (Bakhunu) is recorded in Soninke oral traditions of the Ghana/Wagadu Empire and 19th–20th century French colonial ethnography.
b_bakunu.etymology_analysis: Traditional Soninke province name (Bakhunu / Bakounou) in the Nara/Goumbou region of Mali, south of the Hodh.

b_kita.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kita is attested in Mali Empire historical traditions (associated with Mansa Maghan Keita II, also called Kita Tenin Maghan Keita, c. 1387 CE, and Ibn Khaldun's late 14th-century accounts) and later 19th-century French colonial records.

morphemes.translation: Kita (town and mountain massif in western Mali)

b_kita.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym for the historic town and province at the eastern foot of Mount Kita in western Mali.

b_birgo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Birgo is documented in 19th-century French colonial records (e.g., the French protectorate of Birgo in 1882 CE around Mourgoula) and 20th-century archival studies.
b_birgo.etymology_analysis: Historical Malinke/Fula chiefdom and colonial canton south of Kita in western Mali, centered around Mourgoula.

b_bangasi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bangassi near Kita is documented in 19th–20th century French colonial archives of Mali.
b_bangasi.etymology_analysis: Local Malinke/Khassonké settlement name in the Kayes/Kita region of western Mali, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_banamba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Banamba, a town in the Koulikoro Region of western Mali, is documented in 19th-century pre-colonial and French colonial records (including the 1905–1906 Banamba slave exodus).

morphemes.translation: silk-cotton tree / ceiba (or local settlement root)

b_banamba.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Bambara/Soninke settlement name in the Koulikoro Region of western Mali, historically a Marka/Soninke commercial town north of the Niger River.

b_kolokani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kolokani is documented in modern Malian and French colonial geography of the Bélédougou region.
b_kolokani.etymology_analysis: Bambara town name in the Bélédougou region of Koulikoro, Mali, unattested in medieval written sources.

b_lanba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Lanba is a local Malian toponym without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_lanba.etymology_analysis: Local Mande settlement name in western/central Mali, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kouga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kouga is documented only as a modern Malian locality name.
b_kouga.etymology_analysis: Local Malian toponym in the Middle Niger / Lakes region, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_ras_el-ma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Ra's al-Mā' ('Head of the Water') is first attested in Arabic by al-Bakri in 1068 CE and later in the Tarikh al-Sudan (17th century CE) in connection with Sonni Ali's 1480s canal project.
b_ras_el-ma.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ra's al-Mā' ('Head of the Water'), referring to the western hydrographic extremity of Lake Faguibine in northern Mali.

b_tondiaru.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the megalithic site of Tondidarou (dated archaeologically to 670–790 CE) was first recorded in writing by Jules Brévié in 1904 CE.
b_tondiaru.etymology_analysis: Songhay toponym (Tondidarou / Tondiaru) referring to the standing phalliform stone megaliths on Lake Takadji near Niafunké; the archaeological site dates to c. 670–790 CE, but the name is not contemporarily attested in writing until 1904 CE.

b_dia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; although archaeological excavations at Dia-Shoma show urban occupation from the first millennium BCE, the town name Dia (Ja / Diaka) is first documented in post-867 medieval accounts, oral traditions, and 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles.

morphemes.translation: ancient urban town on the Diaka distributary of the Inner Niger Delta

b_dia.etymology_analysis: Ancient Mande/Soninke/Bozo settlement name (Dia / Ja) on the western margin of Mali's Inner Niger Delta, eponymous center of the Diakhanke clerical-merchant network and the adjacent Diaka distributary.

b_mara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dia-Mara is an archaeological mound in the Dia settlement complex (occupied from the 6th century CE) documented in 20th-century archaeology.

morphemes.translation: Mara (mound site in the Dia complex)

b_mara.etymology_analysis: Modern archaeological and local name for Dia-Mara, one of the three settlement mounds of the Dia complex in the Inner Niger Delta, Mali.

b_shoma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dia-Shoma is an archaeological mound in the Dia complex (occupied from the 9th–6th century BCE) documented in 20th-century archaeology.

morphemes.translation: Shoma (oldest mound site in the Dia complex)

b_shoma.etymology_analysis: Modern archaeological and local name for Dia-Shoma, the largest and oldest mound (49 ha) of the Dia complex in the Inner Niger Delta, Mali.

b_kolima.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kolima is an Iron Age and Stone Age archaeological mound complex and settlement in the Méma region (Niono area) of central Mali, documented only in modern archaeological and geographical surveys.

morphemes.translation: local settlement and archaeological site name in Méma

b_kolima.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Méma alluvial basin of central Mali, associated with prehistoric and Iron Age habitation mounds investigated in modern archaeology.

b_akumbu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Akumbu mound complex in Méma (occupied archaeologically c. 400–1400 CE) is known only from 20th-century archaeological surveys.
b_akumbu.etymology_analysis: Local/archaeological name of the Akumbu iron-working and settlement mound complex in the Méma region of central Mali.

b_toladie.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Toladié (occupied archaeologically c. 430–670 CE) is known only from 20th-century archaeological surveys in Méma.
b_toladie.etymology_analysis: Local/archaeological name of Toladié, a 76-hectare iron-age occupation site in the Méma basin of Mali.

b_boulel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Boulel is known only from modern archaeological surveys of iron-producing sites in Méma.

morphemes.translation: Boulel (settlement and iron-smelting site in Méma)

b_boulel.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Méma region of Mali, documented in modern archaeological literature as an iron-smelting community.

b_west_mema.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; West Mema is a modern directional compound referring to the western portion of the Méma region in central Mali.
b_west_mema.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining English 'West' with the Soninke regional choronym Méma. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_awdaghost.first_mention_attestation: c. 872 CE (first attested as Ghast/Awdaghust by al-Ya'qubi in his Ta'rikh c. 872 CE and Kitab al-Buldan c. 889–891 CE, and later described by Ibn Hawqal c. 977 CE and al-Bakri in 1068 CE — post-dating the 867 CE baseline).

morphemes.translation: historic trans-Saharan caravan oasis city in southern Mauritania

b_awdaghost.etymology_analysis: Sanhaja Berber toponym (Arabic Awdaghust / Ghast; French Aoudaghost) for the renowned medieval trans-Saharan caravan city in southern Mauritania (identified with the ruins of Tegdaoust), first recorded in Arabic historiography shortly after 867 CE.

b_hodh_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Hodh-South is a modern directional compound referring to the southern portion of the Hodh depression in Mauritania.
b_hodh_south.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining Arabic al-ḥawḍ ('basin', denoting the Hodh depression of southeastern Mauritania) with the English directional qualifier 'South'. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_hodh_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Hodh-West is a modern directional compound paralleling modern Hodh El Gharbi in southeastern Mauritania.
b_hodh_west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining Arabic al-ḥawḍ ('basin', denoting the Hodh depression of southeastern Mauritania) with the English directional qualifier 'West'. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_tagant.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tagant is documented in post-medieval Mauritanian oral history and French colonial geography.
b_tagant.etymology_analysis: From Zenaga Berber tagant ('forest'), applied as an oronym to the stony Tagant Plateau of south-central Mauritania.

b_tagant_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Tagant West' is a modern directional compound for an unoccupied holding.
b_tagant_west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining the Berber oronym Tagant with English 'West'.

b_tichitt.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the oasis town of Tichitt was traditionally founded c. 1150 CE (6th century AH) and is recorded in Mauritanian chronicles and UNESCO heritage historiography.

morphemes.translation: Tichitt (oasis town at the foot of the Tagant Plateau)

b_tichitt.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Ticit / Tichitt) for the historic ksar and oasis town in south-central Mauritania, adjacent to the Neolithic Dhar Tichitt escarpment.

b_akrijit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Akreijit is a modern Mauritanian town near the Neolithic Dhar Tichitt archaeological sites.
b_akrijit.etymology_analysis: Local Hassaniya Arabic/Berber name of a town in the Tagant region of central Mauritania, known archaeologically for nearby Neolithic Tichitt-tradition rock art.

b_al-ghaba.first_mention_attestation: 1068 CE (described as al-Ghāba, 'the forest/grove', the walled royal quarter of the capital of the Ghana Empire, in al-Bakri's Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik).
b_al-ghaba.etymology_analysis: Arabic descriptive name al-Ghāba ('the forest' or 'the grove'), applied by Andalusian geographer al-Bakri in 1068 CE to the royal residence quarter of Ghana's twin capital, named for the guarded sacred groves surrounding it that held royal tombs and shrines.

b_niara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Niara is documented only as a modern locality in the Mauritania–Mali borderland.
b_niara.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Hodh/Wagadu borderland between Mauritania and Mali, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bou_khzama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bou Khzama is a modern Mauritanian locality and archaeological site (DN4) in Dhar Néma.
b_bou_khzama.etymology_analysis: Hassaniya Arabic toponym (Bū Khzāma, 'place of lavender/desert herb') in Hodh Ech Chargui, Mauritania, where Neolithic/Iron Age remains have been excavated.

b_kumbi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the name Qunbi (Koumbi) is first attested in the 17th-century Timbuktu chronicle Tarikh al-Fattash (c. 1665 CE), whereas earlier Arabic authors (al-Bakri 1068 CE) referred to the capital simply as Ghāna.

morphemes.translation: Koumbi (capital settlement of the Ghana Empire)

b_kumbi.etymology_analysis: Soninke name (Qunbi / Koumbi) for the archaeological city of Koumbi Saleh in southeastern Mauritania, widely identified as a capital of the Ghana Empire.

historical_names.name: Ghāna
historical_names.notes: Early Arabic geographers referred to the capital/realm of the Ghana Empire simply as Ghāna before Qunbi (Koumbi) was recorded in Tarikh al-Fattash (c. 1665 CE).

b_gumbu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Goumbou (traditionally linked to 7th-century Soninke foundation legends) is recorded only in post-medieval oral tradition and 19th-century colonial accounts.
b_gumbu.etymology_analysis: Soninke town name (Goumbou / Gumbu) in the Ouagadou commune near Nara, Mali.

b_kedama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kédama (Kedama), a desert locality and archaeological site in southeastern Mauritania (Hodh / Dhar Tichitt–Oualata margin), is documented only in modern geographical and archaeological surveys.

morphemes.translation: local desert well and archaeological locality in southeastern Mauritania

b_kedama.etymology_analysis: Local toponym (Kédama) in southeastern Mauritania near the Hodh depression and Dhar escarpments, without pre-modern written attestation.

b_masin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Masin is unattested in medieval Arabic sources.
b_masin.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Wagadu/Hodh region, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_timbedra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Timbedra was founded c. 1904 CE during the French colonial period by members of the Ehel Med Mahmoud (Mechdhouf) family.
b_timbedra.etymology_analysis: Hassaniya Arabic/Berber name of a town in Hodh Ech Chargui, southeastern Mauritania, founded c. 1904 CE.

b_walata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Oualata (Iwalatan / Walāta) is first attested in written sources by Ibn Battuta in 1352 CE, and later in 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles.
b_walata.etymology_analysis: Oasis town in southeastern Mauritania; derived either from Berber Iwalatan or Arabized from Malinke wala ('shady place') after the 15th–17th centuries CE.

b_biru_walata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Biru (Bīru, the earlier Soninke name for Oualata) is attested in 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles such as Tarikh al-Sudan (c. 1655 CE).
b_biru_walata.etymology_analysis: Soninke name Bīru (plural of bire, 'open-sided structure/shelter'), the earlier Mande name of the oasis town later Arabized as Walata.

b_awgham.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Awgham is first attested by Ibn Hawqal in 977 CE (recording Awdaghust's conquest of Awgham in 962 CE).
b_awgham.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sahelian polity/town name recorded in 10th-century Arabic geography (Ibn Hawqal 977 CE), located between Awdaghust and the Niger/Ghana.

b_bura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Bura archaeological site in southwest Niger (dated to c. 200–1300 CE) was only discovered in 1975 CE and excavated from 1983 CE.

morphemes.translation: Bura (modern village and archaeological site in Niger)

b_bura.etymology_analysis: Name of a modern village in Tillabéry Region, Niger, which gave its name to the 3rd–13th century CE Bura archaeological culture.

b_gabou_bura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Gabou in the Bura/Téra region of Niger is documented only in modern geography.
b_gabou_bura.etymology_analysis: Local Nigerien settlement name in the Téra/Bura area, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bilanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Bilanga, a town and department in Gnagna Province of eastern Burkina Faso, is documented only in colonial-era and modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in eastern Burkina Faso

b_bilanga.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Gourmanché/Mossi settlement name in Gnagna Province, eastern Burkina Faso, unattested in pre-modern written sources.

b_sirba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Sirba River is documented in 19th–20th century colonial and modern West African hydrography.

morphemes.translation: Sirba (right-bank tributary of the Niger River)

b_sirba.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Sirba River, flowing from eastern Burkina Faso into the Niger River upstream of Niamey.

b_tondikwarey.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tondikwarey is a modern Zarma/Songhay toponym in western Niger.
b_tondikwarey.etymology_analysis: Zarma/Songhay compound meaning 'White Rock' (tondi 'stone/rock' + kwarey 'white'), a settlement name in western Niger.

b_gurma-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Gurma-West' is a modern directional compound for an unoccupied holding.
b_gurma-west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining the regional name Gurma with English 'West'.

b_nungu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Nungu (Noungou, indigenous name of Fada N'Gourma) is recorded in post-medieval Gourmantché/Mossi oral tradition and 19th-century colonial accounts.
b_nungu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Gourmantché/Mossi name (Nungu / Nũngu) of Fada N'Gourma, capital of the Gourma region in eastern Burkina Faso.

b_tenkudugo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tenkodogo is traditionally dated by oral history to c. 1100 CE as the earliest Mossi kingdom, and recorded in colonial-era writing.
b_tenkudugo.etymology_analysis: Mooré compound meaning 'Ancient Land' (ten- 'land' + kudugo 'ancient'), capital of the historic Mossi kingdom of Tenkodogo in Burkina Faso.

b_say.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Say on the Niger River rose in the 19th century CE as an Islamic scholarly center founded by Alfa Mohamed Diobo.

morphemes.translation: Say (town on the Niger River in southwestern Niger)

b_say.etymology_analysis: Town on the Niger River in Tillabéry Region, Niger, historically prominent from the 19th century CE.

b_burunfongo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Burunfongo is a local toponym in the Niger–Burkina Faso borderland without medieval written attestation.
b_burunfongo.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Lower Gurma / Niger River borderland, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_aribinda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Aribinda (Arbinda), a town and department in Soum Province of northern Burkina Faso, is documented in late 19th-century European accounts and colonial administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in northern Burkina Faso

b_aribinda.etymology_analysis: Local Kurumba/Songhai settlement toponym (Arbinda / Aribinda) in the Sahel Region of northern Burkina Faso, unattested in medieval written sources.

b_burzanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bourzanga (featuring a Kurumba royal necropolis) is documented only in 20th-century archaeology and modern Burkinabé geography.

morphemes.translation: Bourzanga (town in Bam Province, Burkina Faso)

b_burzanga.etymology_analysis: Town in Bam Province, northern Burkina Faso, noted for its Kurumba royal necropolis of 109 stelae.

b_mergao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Mergao is a local settlement name in northern Burkina Faso without medieval written attestation.
b_mergao.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in northern Burkina Faso (Kurumba/Upper Gurma area), unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_kissi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kissi, a locality and Iron Age archaeological cemetery complex near the Mare de Kissi in Oudalan Province of northern Burkina Faso, is documented only in modern geographical and archaeological surveys.

morphemes.translation: local settlement and archaeological site name in Oudalan

b_kissi.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in Oudalan Province, northern Burkina Faso, known for Iron Age burial mounds excavated near the seasonal Mare de Kissi; the toponym itself has no pre-867 written attestation.

b_dinde.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dinde is a local settlement name in the Oudalan/Sahel borderland without medieval written attestation.
b_dinde.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Oudalan/Upper Gurma borderland, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_oursi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological mound complexes around Oursi date to the 1st–2nd millennium CE, and the modern settlement is documented in colonial/post-colonial French West African records.

morphemes.translation: local toponym of Oudalan settlement and adjacent Mare d'Oursi

b_oursi.etymology_analysis: Oursi is a Sahelian toponym in Oudalan Province, northern Burkina Faso, associated with the adjacent Mare d'Oursi wetland and archaeological settlement mounds occupied during the 1st and early 2nd millennia CE before abandonment around 1400 CE.

b_saouga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological mound complexes at Saouga date to the 1st–2nd millennium CE, while written documentation of the commune is modern.
b_saouga.etymology_analysis: Saouga is a village and commune in Gorom-Gorom Department, Oudalan Province, Burkina Faso, known archaeologically for Iron Age settlement mounds occupied during the 1st to 14th centuries CE.

b_dori.first_mention_attestation: 1853 CE (visited and documented by Heinrich Barth during his Sahelian expedition; Dori served as capital of the Fula Emirate of Liptako founded in 1810 CE).

morphemes.translation: market town and capital of Liptako

b_dori.etymology_analysis: Dori is the historic capital of the Fula Emirate of Liptako (established 1810 CE) in northeastern Burkina Faso; its written attestation begins in 19th-century CE European travelogues such as Heinrich Barth's 1853 CE account.

b_gurma-rharous.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Gourma-Rharous (also Gurma-Rharous or Rharous), a town on the right bank of the Niger Bend in Mali, is documented in post-medieval and French colonial records.

morphemes.translation: right/south bank of the Niger Bend (Gourma region)
local riverine settlement name on the Niger Bend

b_gurma-rharous.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym combining Gourma (the Songhai regional designation for the right/south bank of the Niger Bend) with the local Tamasheq/Songhai settlement name Rharous. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a compound settlement locator.

b_zampia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Zampia is a modern archaeological designation (Zampia ceramic facies of the Windé Koroji Complex near Douentza, 1st millennium BCE, excavated 1993–1996 CE).

morphemes.translation: site name near Douentza in southern Gourma

b_zampia.etymology_analysis: Zampia is a modern archaeological site/facies name in the Windé Koroji Complex north of Douentza in southern Gourma, Mali, associated with first-millennium BCE pastoralist tumuli and stone alignments.

b_hombori.first_mention_attestation: Early 17th century CE (c. 1600s CE Songhai/Timbuktu chronicle traditions and Ahmad Baba's references to Hombori).

morphemes.translation: town at the foot of Hombori Tondo

b_hombori.etymology_analysis: Hombori (local Songhai Humburi) is a town in the Douentza area of central Mali situated beneath the Hombori Tondo massif; it became a refuge and strategic point for Songhai royal refugees after the 1591 CE Moroccan invasion.

b_bandiagara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Dogon settlement of the Bandiagara Escarpment dates from c. 14th–15th century CE, with written documentation in the 19th–20th century CE.
b_bandiagara.etymology_analysis: Derived from the archaic Dogon term bàndʒà-gàrá, meaning 'large wooden eating bowl', referring to ceremonial wooden bowls crafted by blacksmiths. The Dogon migrated to the escarpment around the 14th–15th century CE, succeeding the Tellem (11th–16th century CE).

b_ounjougou.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Ounjougou is a modern lieu-dit discovered archaeologically in 1994 CE (with Paleolithic, Early Holocene pottery c. 9400 BCE, and pre-Dogon deposits).

morphemes.translation: local lieu-dit in the Upper Yamé Valley

b_ounjougou.etymology_analysis: Ounjougou is a Dogon lieu-dit in the Upper Yamé Valley on the Bandiagara Plateau, Mali, famous since 1994 CE excavations for yielding some of the earliest pottery in Africa (c. 9400 BCE) and a long pre-Dogon sequence.

b_douentza.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Douentza, a town in central Mali (Mopti / Douentza Region), is documented from 19th-century pre-colonial and French colonial administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name at the foot of the Gandamia massif

b_douentza.etymology_analysis: Indigenous settlement name in central Mali along the corridor between Mopti and Gao, without pre-modern written attestation.

b_samyere.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Gondo plain

b_samyere.etymology_analysis: Samyere is a local settlement name in the Gondo/Douentza area of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_bankass.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Bankass, a town in central Mali on the Séno plain within Dogon country, is documented only in colonial-era and modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name on the Séno plain

b_bankass.etymology_analysis: Indigenous settlement toponym on the Séno-Gondo plain in central Mali (Mopti / Bandiagara Region), unattested in medieval written sources.

b_douna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern written sources <= 867 CE; Douna (Douentza Cercle, Mopti Region) is a modern rural commune/village attested in 20th-century Malian administrative records (distinct from the homonymous Bani River hydrometric station).
b_douna.etymology_analysis: Douna is a village in central Mali (Douentza/Séno area, and also a homonymous hydrometric station on the Bani River recorded from 1922 CE), lacking pre-modern written attestation.

b_seno-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Seno-South is a modern directional compound referring to the southern portion of the Séno sandy plain in central Mali.
b_seno-south.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining Fulfulde séno ('sandy plain', referring to the Séno-Gondo plain) with the English directional qualifier 'South'. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_giti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Giti (also linked with Rawatenga), an early Mossi locality in Yatenga, northern Burkina Faso, is known from post-medieval Mossi oral traditions and modern historical/ethnographic records.
b_giti.etymology_analysis: Local Mossi/Mooré toponym in Yatenga, northern Burkina Faso, associated in oral tradition with early 15th–16th-century Mossi state formation under Naaba Rawa and Naaba Yadega.

b_walguyo.first_mention_attestation: 1757 CE (founded as Ouahigouya / Wayugyã by Naaba Kango as the capital of the Kingdom of Yatenga).

morphemes.translation: come and pay homage / bow down

b_walguyo.etymology_analysis: Walguyo represents Ouahigouya (Mooré Wayugyã), founded in 1757 CE by Naaba Kango as the capital of Yatenga; the Mooré name means 'come and pay homage'.

b_zondoma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Zondoma is a Mossi kingdom/province (traditionally founded by Rawa, son of Ouédraogo) documented in colonial and modern historical works.

morphemes.translation: historic Mossi polity and province centered on Gourcy

b_zondoma.etymology_analysis: Zondoma (also Zandoma) is a historic Mossi kingdom and modern province in northern Burkina Faso with its seat at Gourcy, documented in oral tradition and post-19th-century written historiography.

b_gursi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Gourcy (Gursi) was the early seat of Yatenga before 1757 CE and is documented in colonial/post-colonial records.

morphemes.translation: historic town and capital of Zondoma

b_gursi.etymology_analysis: Gursi (French Gourcy) is the historic Mossi town in Zondoma Province from which Yatenga rulers expanded in the 16th century CE before relocating the capital to Ouahigouya in 1757 CE.

b_rim.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological sites Rim I–III show occupation from c. 3000 BCE and ironworking in the 6th–10th centuries CE, while the village name is modern.

morphemes.translation: village and archaeological complex in Koumbri Department

b_rim.etymology_analysis: Rim is a village in Koumbri Department, Yatenga Province, Burkina Faso, notable archaeologically for the Rim I–III prehistoric and early iron-metallurgy sites (6th–10th centuries CE), though the toponym itself has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Dogon settlement at Sangha/Sanga dates to the 14th–15th centuries CE, and Sanga in Yatenga (Thiou) is documented in modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in Dogon Country / Yatenga

b_sanga.etymology_analysis: Sanga (Sangha in Mali, or Sanga in Thiou Department, Yatenga) is a regional settlement name; the Dogon cultural center of Sangha was settled around the 14th–15th centuries CE.

b_biun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in eastern Burkina Faso

b_biun.etymology_analysis: Biun is a local toponym in the Gurma/Tapoa region of eastern Burkina Faso without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_gobnangou.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern geographical and administrative sources (including the 2025 CE Gobnangou Province reform).

morphemes.translation: sandstone cliff / escarpment range in southeastern Burkina Faso

b_gobnangou.etymology_analysis: Gobnangou is an oronym referring to the Chaîne de Gobnangou sandstone escarpment in southeastern Burkina Faso, which also gives its name to the surrounding province.

b_pentenga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Pentenga is a modern archaeological rock-shelter site in southeastern Burkina Faso.
b_pentenga.etymology_analysis: Pentenga is a rock-shelter archaeological site in southeastern Burkina Faso (alongside Yobri and Maadaga) known for Paleolithic/Holocene stone industries, lacking pre-modern written attestation.

b_bena.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Bena (Béna / Béné), a locality in the Bobo/Bwa borderland between Mali and Burkina Faso, is documented only in modern administrative and ethnographic records.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Mali–Burkina Faso borderland

b_bena.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Bobo/Bwa settlement toponym in the borderland between southeastern Mali and western Burkina Faso, without pre-modern written attestation.

b_dourola.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological iron-smelting furnaces near Douroula date to the 8th century BCE, while the town name is documented in modern records.

morphemes.translation: town in Mouhoun Province, Burkina Faso

b_dourola.etymology_analysis: Dourola (Douroula) is a town in Mouhoun Province, western Burkina Faso, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for nearby 8th-century BCE iron-smelting furnaces, though the town name is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_sikasso.first_mention_attestation: 1876 CE (made capital of the Kénédougou Kingdom by Tieba Traoré; besieged by Samori Touré in 1887–1888 CE and documented in French colonial records).
b_sikasso.etymology_analysis: Settlement name in southern Mali incorporating the Manding element -so ('house/village'); rose to prominence in 1876 CE as the fortified capital of the Kénédougou Kingdom.

b_kumya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in southern Mali

b_kumya.etymology_analysis: Kumya is a local settlement name in the Sikasso/Bobo borderland of southern Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_baninko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Baninko is a historic Bambara region in Mali documented in modern ethnographic and historical literature.
b_baninko.etymology_analysis: Baninko is a historic Bambara region in Mali meaning 'beyond/behind the Bani (river)', a locator compound excluded from natural_proper_name.

b_soum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Soum, a locality and province in northern Burkina Faso named after the seasonal Mare de Soum wetland, is documented only in colonial-era and modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: seasonal pool/wetland (Mare de Soum) in northern Burkina Faso

b_soum.etymology_analysis: Directly named after the Mare de Soum, a prominent seasonal lake and pastoral waterhole in northern Burkina Faso that gave its name to the surrounding locality and province.

b_taba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Bani/Ségou basin

b_taba.etymology_analysis: Taba is a local settlement name in the Bindugu/Ségou area of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_san.first_mention_attestation: 1690 CE (conquered by Biton Coulibaly of the Bamana Empire; earlier 1542 CE Songhai raid targeted 'Sama', which may refer to Sama Foulala rather than San).

morphemes.translation: market town near the Bani River

b_san.etymology_analysis: San is a historic market town in central Mali near the Bani River; local tradition links its founding to the sanké pond, toro fig tree, and karantéla well, and it entered written history in the 17th–19th centuries CE.

b_segou.first_mention_attestation: 1796 CE (recorded by Scottish explorer Mungo Park during his 1796 visit to Ségou on the Niger River; traditionally founded c. 1620 CE by Bozo fishermen and established as capital of the Bambara Empire in 1712 CE).

morphemes.translation: Ségou (historic city on the Niger River)

b_segou.etymology_analysis: From Bambara Ségu (French Ségou), a major city on the Niger River in south-central Mali founded around 1620 CE by Bozo fishermen and famed as the capital of the 18th-century Bambara Empire.

b_kri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kri/Kiri is attested in Mandinka oral traditions (13th century CE Sunyata epic) and modern historiography of the Mali Empire.
b_kri.etymology_analysis: Kri (Kiri) is one of the core constituent provinces of Manden (alongside Do/Dodougou) in the 13th-century CE Mali Empire formation traditions, associated with the Traoré clan.

b_niamina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in colonial/modern Malian geographical records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name along the Niger River in Koulikoro/Ségou

b_niamina.etymology_analysis: Niamina is a riverine town in Mali along the Niger River between Koulikoro and Ségou, lacking pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tamani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Malian administrative records.

morphemes.translation: small talking drum / town name in Barouéli Cercle

b_tamani.etymology_analysis: Tamani is a town and commune in Barouéli Cercle, Ségou Region, Mali (homonymous with the Bambara tamani talking drum), without pre-modern written attestation.

b_sanado.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in central Mali

b_sanado.etymology_analysis: Sanado is a local settlement name in the Ségou/Dodugu region of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_jenne-jeno.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; while archaeological excavations show the urban mound of Jenné-Jeno (Djenné-Djenno) was occupied from c. 250 BCE to c. 1400 CE, the name Jenné-Jeno ('ancient/old Djenné') is a modern Bozo and archaeological designation (modern Djenné itself is first attested in writing in 1447 CE by Antonio Malfante as 'Geni').

morphemes.translation: Djenné (historic Inner Niger Delta urban center)

b_jenne-jeno.etymology_analysis: Bozo toponym (Djenné-Djenno / Jenné-Jeno) meaning 'ancient Djenné' or 'old Djenné', referring to the abandoned archaeological tell 3 km southeast of modern Djenné in Mali's Inner Niger Delta. Despite pre-867 urban occupation, the name itself is unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE.

b_kaniana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kaniana is an archaeological tell near Djenné excavated in 1981 CE and inscribed as part of UNESCO's Old Towns of Djenné in 1988 CE.
b_kaniana.etymology_analysis: Kaniana is one of the four archaeological tell sites comprising the Old Towns of Djenné in the Inland Niger Delta, Mali, lacking pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_mopti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Mopti grew from a Bozo fishing village in the 19th–20th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: gathering place / confluence settlement at the Niger-Bani junction

b_mopti.etymology_analysis: Mopti (Fulfulde Mobti) is located at the confluence of the Niger and Bani rivers in central Mali; it developed into a major town in the 19th–20th centuries CE without pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kiri-bara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.
b_kiri-bara.etymology_analysis: Kiri-Bara is a compound toponym in the Inland Niger Delta / Djenné area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_korienza.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Korientzé (Korienza), a town near Lake Korientzé in the Mopti Region of central Mali, is documented only in colonial-era and modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: town in the Inner Niger Delta margin of Mopti Region

b_korienza.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym (Korientzé / Korienza) in the Mopti Region of central Mali, seat of the rural commune of Korombana near Lake Korientzé.

b_bangu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: pond, floodplain depression, or local settlement

b_bangu.etymology_analysis: Bangu is a local Malian toponym in the Kurmina/Niger Bend area (cf. Songhai bangu 'pond/lake') without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_safare.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Inland Niger Delta

b_safare.etymology_analysis: Safare is a local settlement name in the Kurmina/Inland Niger Delta area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_nguma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Inland Niger Delta

b_nguma.etymology_analysis: Nguma is a local settlement name in the Kurmina/Inland Niger Delta area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_niamina_jara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Niamina, a historic Mandinka province/kingdom on the south bank of the middle Gambia River, is documented in early modern European river-trade accounts and 19th-century British colonial records.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka province on the Gambia River

b_niamina_jara.etymology_analysis: Mandinka polity and district name (Niamina, today comprising Niamina East, Niamina West, and Niamina Dankunku in the Central River Region of The Gambia), attested only in post-medieval European and colonial sources.

b_kiang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kiang is documented in post-16th-century European maps and colonial Gambian records as a Mandinka kingdom.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River

b_kiang.etymology_analysis: Kiang was a pre-colonial Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River (now Kiang West, Central, and East districts in The Gambia), attested only in early modern and colonial sources.

b_pakao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Pakao is documented in Mandinka oral traditions, the Ajami Pakao Book, and colonial Senegalese records.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka province in middle Casamance

b_pakao.etymology_analysis: Pakao is a historic Mandinka cultural and Islamic scholarly region in the middle Casamance (Sédhiou region, Senegal), documented in post-medieval oral traditions and Ajami manuscripts.

b_achum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Achum, a locality near the Geba basin in Guinea-Bissau, is documented only in modern geographical records.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name near Geba in Guinea-Bissau

b_achum.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in the Geba region of Guinea-Bissau without pre-modern written attestation.

b_birasu.first_mention_attestation: c. 1506 CE (Valentim Fernandes, Description de la Côte Occidentale d'Afrique, mentioning the faran of Birasu).

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka-ruled kingdom between the Casamance and Cacheu rivers

b_birasu.etymology_analysis: Birasu (also Braço / Birassu) was a Mandinka kingdom in the Kaabu/Casamance sphere, first attested in writing around 1506 CE by Valentim Fernandes.

b_mansoa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; the Mansôa town grew from a 19th-century CE Portuguese trading post on the Mansoa River (permanent military post 1913 CE).

morphemes.translation: major river and town in central Guinea-Bissau

b_mansoa.etymology_analysis: Mansoa (Mansôa) is named after the Mansoa River in central Guinea-Bissau; the modern town developed from a 19th-century CE Portuguese trading post.

b_guinala.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (1583 CE Portuguese retreat to a fort at Guinala; also documented in late 16th-century CE accounts by André Álvares de Almada as a Biafada kingdom).

morphemes.translation: Biafada kingdom and port on the Rio Grande de Buba (also Quinara)

b_guinala.etymology_analysis: Guinala (also Quinara) was a major pre-colonial Biafada kingdom and trading port between the Geba and Rio Grande de Buba rivers, attested in 16th-century CE Portuguese sources.

b_kombo.first_mention_attestation: 1621 CE (documented by English explorer Richard Jobson in 1621 CE and Portuguese chronicler André Donelha in 1625 CE as a Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River mouth).

morphemes.translation: historic coastal kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River

b_kombo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mandinka kingdom and region name (Kombo) on the Atlantic coast south of the Gambia River estuary, attested from early 17th-century European accounts.

b_fogny.first_mention_attestation: Late 16th century CE (c. 1594 CE André Álvares de Almada, Tratado Breve dos Rios de Guiné, mentioning the king of Fogni; earlier 15th-century Bainuk state).

morphemes.translation: region between the Gambia and Casamance rivers

b_fogny.etymology_analysis: Fogny (also Foni, Fooñi) is a geographic and historical region in the Casamance shared between Senegal and The Gambia, attested in 16th-century CE Portuguese sources.

b_bainuk.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (Portuguese accounts rendering the name as 'Banyun', and Mandinka oral history from Pakao).
b_bainuk.etymology_analysis: Bainuk (also Banyun, Bainouk) is an ethnonym for the early inhabitants of the lower Casamance, first recorded in 16th-century CE Portuguese sources; Mandinka oral etymology links it to Mandinka bai ('chase away').

b_kasa.first_mention_attestation: 1456 CE (mid-15th-century Portuguese navigators trading with the Mansa of Kasa, giving the Casamance River its name).
b_kasa.etymology_analysis: Bainuk/Jola/Mandinka kingdom name (Kasa / Kasanga) in lower Casamance, whose ruler's title Kasa mansa ('King of Kasa') gave rise to the name Casamance.

b_bijagos.first_mention_attestation: Mid-15th century CE (1456 CE Portuguese/Venetian coastal voyages of Alvise Cadamosto and Diogo Gomes).

morphemes.translation: archipelago and island group off the coast of Guinea-Bissau

b_bijagos.etymology_analysis: Bijagos (Bijagós Islands) is the Atlantic deltaic archipelago off Guinea-Bissau inhabited by the Bijago people, first documented by European navigators in the mid-15th century CE.

b_pepel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in early modern Portuguese and colonial Guinea-Bissau sources (16th–19th centuries CE).

morphemes.translation: ethnic group and territory of Bissau and Biombo

b_pepel.etymology_analysis: Pepel (Papel) is an ethnonym for the coastal Bak-speaking people of the Bissau region in Guinea-Bissau, unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_jagara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; possibly a variant of Jarra/Jagra (attested 1732 CE) or Senegambian title jagaraf, with no pre-867 written attestation.
b_jagara.etymology_analysis: Jagara is an unoccupied barony slot in the Kasa/Senegambia region (cf. Jagra/Jarra or Senegambian title jagaraf), lacking any contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_niumi.first_mention_attestation: 1455–1456 CE (recorded by Venetian explorer Alvise Cadamosto as 'Gnumimenssa', referring to the Niumi Mansa or King of Niumi, and shortly thereafter by Diogo Gomes as 'Nomyans').

morphemes.translation: historic kingdom at the mouth of the Gambia River

b_niumi.etymology_analysis: Mandinka-Serer kingdom name (Niumi, also known to European traders as Barra) at the northern mouth of the Gambia River, first attested in mid-15th-century European maritime accounts.

b_badibu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Badibu (Baddibu) is documented in early modern European riverine trade and colonial Gambian records.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka kingdom on the north bank of the Gambia River

b_badibu.etymology_analysis: Badibu (Baddibu) was a pre-colonial Mandinka state on the north bank of the Gambia River (now Lower, Central, and Upper Baddibu districts), unattested <= 867 CE.

b_saalum.first_mention_attestation: c. 1494 CE (foundation of the Serer Kingdom of Saloum by Mbegan Ndour in Senegalese historiography and early modern European accounts).

morphemes.translation: historic Serer kingdom in central Senegal

b_saalum.etymology_analysis: Serer toponym (Saalum / Saluum, French Saloum) for the pre-colonial Serer kingdom founded around 1494 CE in central Senegal, unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_kahone.first_mention_attestation: c. 1494 CE (established as the royal capital of the Kingdom of Saloum; documented in early modern European and colonial Senegalese sources).

morphemes.translation: pre-colonial capital of the Kingdom of Saloum

b_kahone.etymology_analysis: Kahone is a town near Kaolack in Senegal that served as the royal capital of the Kingdom of Saloum from its foundation c. 1494 CE, unattested <= 867 CE.

b_pakala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Pakala is documented as a canton/province of the Kingdom of Saloum in colonial and modern Senegalese records.

morphemes.translation: historic canton in the Saloum/Kaolack region

b_pakala.etymology_analysis: Pakala is a historic canton and village in the Kaolack/Saloum region of Senegal without pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_gabou.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (independent Kaabu/Gabú federation established c. 1537 CE, following 13th-century CE Mali Empire expansion traditions and 15th–16th-century CE Portuguese accounts).

morphemes.translation: Kaabu / Gabú imperial province and federation

b_gabou.etymology_analysis: Variant spelling of Kaabu (Portuguese Gabú, French Gabou), a Mandinka western province of the Mali Empire (13th century CE) that became an independent federation in 1537 CE and gave its name to the modern city and region of Gabú in eastern Guinea-Bissau.

b_bajar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Badiar/Pajadi appears in later regional oral traditions (such as the 16th-century CE campaigns of Koli Tenguella) and modern Guinean-Senegalese toponymy (Badiar National Park, established 1985 CE).

morphemes.translation: ethnonym/toponym of the Badyaranke people and region

b_bajar.etymology_analysis: Derived from the indigenous West African toponym and ethnonym Bajar (also spelled Badiar or Pajadi), associated with the Badyaranke (Bajaranke) people of the Guinea-Senegal borderlands. No written attestation exists prior to 867 CE.

b_kensala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kansala is known from Mandinka oral traditions as the capital of Kaabu (founded after the 13th-century CE Mandinka expansion) and is documented in 19th-century CE accounts of the Battle of Kansala (1867 CE).
b_kensala.etymology_analysis: Mandinka toponym for the fortified capital of the Kaabu confederation in northeastern Guinea-Bissau, traditionally established by Mansa Sala Sane after the 13th century CE and destroyed in 1867 CE.

b_toumana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tumana (Toumana) is attested in later Mandinka oral traditions and European accounts as one of the constituent provinces of the Kaabu federation (13th-19th centuries CE).
b_toumana.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mandinka territorial name for a core province of the Kaabu Empire in the upper Casamance/Gambia-Guinea-Bissau borderlands.

b_pakane.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Pakane (Pachana/Pakane) is associated with the post-13th-century CE Mandinka provinces of Kaabu.
b_pakane.etymology_analysis: Mandinka provincial toponym within the Kaabu cultural sphere of southern Senegambia and Guinea-Bissau, without written attestation before 867 CE.

b_wuli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Wuli (Woolli) is dated by oral tradition to the mid-13th century CE Mandinka expansion under Tiramakhan Traore and appears in European records from the 15th-16th centuries CE onward.

morphemes.translation: historical Mandinka kingdom on the north bank of the Gambia River

b_wuli.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mandinka toponym for the kingdom on the north bank of the upper Gambia River (spelled Wuli, Woolli, or Ouli in European sources).

b_kantor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kantora (Kantor) is attested in later Mandinka oral traditions and European records as a province of Kaabu on the south bank of the upper Gambia River.

morphemes.translation: easternmost Mandinka province along the upper Gambia

b_kantor.etymology_analysis: Mandinka territorial name for the easternmost district of The Gambia and adjacent Senegal, historically a tributary province of Kaabu.

b_naani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Mandinka Kingdom of Niani on the north bank of the Gambia River existed from approximately the 14th to the late 19th century CE.

morphemes.translation: historical Mandinka kingdom on the north bank of the Gambia

b_naani.etymology_analysis: Mandinka toponym for the Gambian kingdom of Niani (distinct from Niani in Guinea), attested from the 14th century CE onward.

b_yaresna.first_mention_attestation: 1068 CE (recorded as Yaresnā, a Muslim trading town on the upper Senegal / Falémé gold-trade route, in al-Bakri's Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik).

morphemes.translation: historic trading town on the upper Senegal/Falémé

b_yaresna.etymology_analysis: Medieval West African toponym (Arabic transcription Yaresnā, sometimes identified with Barīsā) for an important Muslim trading town near the upper Senegal and Falémé rivers linked to the Bambuk gold trade, first recorded by al-Bakri in 1068 CE.

b_goundafa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Goundafa is a modern village and hill locality in the Tambacounda Region of eastern Senegal.

morphemes.translation: local settlement and hill toponym in Tambacounda

b_goundafa.etymology_analysis: Local Senegalese toponym in the Tambacounda Region near the Mali border, lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_diouboye.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; although archaeological excavations at Diouboye along the Falémé River show occupation from c. 500 to 1400 CE, the name Diouboye itself is modern local toponymy.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name on the Falémé River

b_diouboye.etymology_analysis: Modern toponym of an archaeological site on the Falémé River in eastern Senegal; despite first-millennium CE habitation, no contemporary written source records this name before 867 CE.

b_ghiyaru.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1068 CE by the Andalusian geographer al-Bakri as Ghiyaru, a densely populated gold-producing center 18 days' travel from the capital of Ghana.

morphemes.translation: historical gold-trading town (often identified with Goundiourou)

b_ghiyaru.etymology_analysis: Arabic transcription (Ghiyaru) recorded by al-Bakri in 1068 CE for an indigenous Soninke/Mande settlement, frequently identified by historians with Goundiourou near Kayes on the Senegal River.

b_bundu.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1690 CE by the Fula Torodbe cleric Malick Sy; documented in 18th- and 19th-century CE European travel accounts (such as Daniel Houghton 1791 CE and Mungo Park 1795 CE).
b_bundu.etymology_analysis: From Pulaar bundu ('well'), referring to the pre-colonial Fula state established in the late 17th century CE between the Falémé and upper Gambia rivers.

b_tenda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Tenda region and river-crossing communities in southeastern Senegal are documented in external records from the 17th century CE onward.
b_tenda.etymology_analysis: From Mandinka tenda ('landing place' or 'wharf'), reflecting the region's role as a major caravan fording zone across the upper Gambia River.

b_niokolo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Niokolo (Niokolo-Koba) is documented in 20th-century CE colonial and Senegalese records (established as a reserve in 1925 CE and national park in 1954 CE).

morphemes.translation: local river and territorial name in southeastern Senegal

b_niokolo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym of the upper Gambia tributary basin in southeastern Senegal (Niokolo-Koba), without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_damantan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Damantan is a modern locality in southeastern Senegal.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in eastern Senegal

b_damantan.etymology_analysis: Local Senegalese settlement toponym lacking any written attestation prior to 867 CE.

b_busura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Busura is a modern settlement toponym in the Senegambia/Bundu borderlands.
b_busura.etymology_analysis: West African settlement toponym in the upper Senegal/Gambia region, unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_badumbe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Badoumbé (Badumbe), a village and former colonial post on the Bakoye River in Kayes Region, Mali, is documented in late 19th-century French colonial and Dakar–Niger railway records.

morphemes.translation: settlement on the Bakoye River in Bafoulabé Cercle

b_badumbe.etymology_analysis: Local Malinke/Kassonke settlement name (Badoumbé) on the left bank of the Bakoye River in western Mali, attested only in colonial-era and modern records.

b_nyeningo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Nyeningo is a local Malian toponym without pre-867 CE written records.

morphemes.translation: local settlement toponym in western Mali

b_nyeningo.etymology_analysis: Local Mande settlement name in the Gangaran/Kayes area of western Mali, unattested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_bafulabe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bafoulabé is documented in French colonial records from 1880 CE (captured by Joseph Gallieni) and became the first cercle in Mali in 1887 CE.
b_bafulabe.etymology_analysis: From Bambara/Malinke ba-fula-be ('meeting of two rivers'), referring to the confluence of the Bafing and Bakoy rivers that form the Senegal River.

b_kunjan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Koundian appears in 13th-century CE Malian oral tradition (associated with Moussa-Son-Koroma Sissoko) and 19th-century CE French accounts of its Tukolor fortress.
b_kunjan.etymology_analysis: Malinke settlement name (also spelled Kunjan or Koundian) in southwestern Mali, known for its 19th-century CE tata fortification.

b_konko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Konkodougou (Konko) is attested in 14th-century CE Mali Empire historiography (Mansa Konkodougou Kamissa Keita, crowned 1360 CE).

morphemes.translation: mountain, hill, or historical province name

b_konko.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym (shortened from Konkodougou) for a historical province of the Mali Empire in the Bambuk/upper Senegal borderlands.

b_sangalan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Sangalan is documented in Dialonka oral traditions and 19th-century CE historical records (emerging as an independent federation after 1850 CE).

morphemes.translation: Dialonka federation territory in northeastern Guinea

b_sangalan.etymology_analysis: Dialonka territorial name for a federation of villages in northeastern Guinea (Mali-Yambering region), documented in 19th-century CE and oral historical sources.

b_upper_gambia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Upper Gambia is a modern English geographic compound designating the upper reaches of the Gambia River (the river name Gambia itself is first attested in 15th-century Portuguese accounts, e.g., 1455 CE).
b_upper_gambia.etymology_analysis: Modern English geographic compound combining 'Upper' with the hydronym Gambia (adopted via Portuguese from indigenous Senegambian river names such as Kambra/Kambaa). Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_woora_saabe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Woora Saabe is a local West African toponym without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_woora_saabe.etymology_analysis: Compound West African toponym from the upper Gambia / Fouta Djallon borderlands, unattested in written sources before 867 CE.

b_kaade.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kadé (Kaade), a historic settlement and district in the northwestern Fouta Djallon borderlands of Guinea, is documented in 19th-century Imamate of Futa Jallon and French colonial records.

morphemes.translation: settlement and province name in northwestern Guinea

b_kaade.etymology_analysis: Indigenous settlement and district name (Kadé / Kaade) in northwestern Guinea near the Fouta Djallon–Guinea-Bissau borderlands, historically subordinate to Labé.

b_bambaya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bambaya is a modern settlement name in Guinea without pre-867 CE written records.
b_bambaya.etymology_analysis: Guinean settlement toponym (from Mande/Susu naming patterns with the locative/clan suffix -ya), unattested before 867 CE.

b_waasu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Waasu is a local toponym in the Fouta Djallon / Kokoli region without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_waasu.etymology_analysis: Local West African toponym in Guinea, lacking any written attestation by 867 CE.

b_geme.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Guémé-Sangan (Geme) is associated with early 16th-century CE oral traditions of Koli Tenguella (c. 1512 CE) near Télimélé in Guinea.
b_geme.etymology_analysis: From Guémé (Guémé-Sangan), the rocky fortress and cave site near Télimélé in Guinea where Koli Tenguella is said to have regrouped his forces around 1512 CE.

b_timbi_tunni.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Timbi (Timbi-Touny / Timbi-Madina) is documented in Fouta Djallon history from the 18th-century CE Imamate and colonial periods onward.

morphemes.translation: historical plateau province in central Fouta Djallon

b_timbi_tunni.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym of the Timbi plateau in the Pita Prefecture of central Guinea (including Timbi-Touny and Timbi-Madina).

b_kula.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kula is a local toponym in the Fouta Djallon region without pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in Fouta Djallon

b_kula.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in the Fouta Djallon highlands of Guinea, unattested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_kompela.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kompela is a local toponym in the Fouta Djallon region without pre-867 CE written records.
b_kompela.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in the Timbi/Fouta Djallon area of Guinea, lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_ndama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Ndama (N'Dama) is known in modern times as a highland area and forest in northwestern Guinea (part of the Badiar Biosphere Reserve) and as the namesake of N'Dama cattle.

morphemes.translation: highland and forest region in northwestern Guinea

b_ndama.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Ndama forest and plateau in northwestern Guinea, associated with the trypanotolerant N'Dama cattle breed.

b_labe.first_mention_attestation: c. 1720s CE (founded in the 1720s by Fulani/Dialonke settlers and named after their chief Manga Labé, becoming a principal province of the Imamate of Futa Jallon).

eponym.details: Named after Manga Labé (early 18th century CE), the Fulani/Dialonke chief credited with founding the town in the 1720s.

morphemes.translation: personal name of 18th-century founder Manga Labé

b_labe.etymology_analysis: Named after Manga Labé, the chief who founded the town in the 1720s during the rise of the Islamic Imamate of Futa Jallon in north-central Guinea.

b_kokunya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kokunya is a local toponym in the Fouta Djallon region without pre-867 CE written records.
b_kokunya.etymology_analysis: Local Guinean settlement toponym in the Fouta Djallon highlands, unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_timbo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Timbo became the capital of the Imamate of Futa Jallon under Karamokho Alfa between 1727 and 1751 CE and appears in 18th- and 19th-century CE accounts.

morphemes.translation: historic capital town of the Imamate of Futa Jallon

b_timbo.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the historic capital of the Imamate of Futa Jallon in Mamou Prefecture, central Guinea, prominent from the early 18th century CE.

b_upper_bafing.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; 'Upper Bafing' is a modern English geographic compound referring to the upper course of the Bafing River in Guinea.
b_upper_bafing.etymology_analysis: English directional/locator compound ('Upper') combined with Manding ba-fing ('black river'), the upper course of the Senegal River.

b_falanko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Falanko, a settlement and stream locality in the Kissidougou area of southeastern Guinea, is documented only in modern geographical records.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Kissidougou area

b_falanko.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in the Kissi/Kissidougou area of Guinea's Forest Region, without pre-modern written attestation.

b_kisi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; the Kissi (Kisi) people and territory spanning southeastern Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia are documented in European and colonial records from the early modern and 19th-century CE periods onward.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and territory of the Kissi people

b_kisi.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and territorial designation of the Kissi people of southeastern Guinea, eastern Sierra Leone, and northern Liberia.

b_mara_kisi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Mara is a local toponym in the Kissi/Guinea highlands without pre-867 CE written records.
b_mara_kisi.etymology_analysis: Local West African toponym in the Kissi region of Guinea/Sierra Leone, unattested in written sources before 867 CE.

b_lele.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Lele are a Mande-speaking group in Guinea documented in modern ethnographic classifications.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and territory of the Lele people of Guinea

b_lele.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Mande-speaking Lele people of eastern/forest Guinea, lacking any pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kuranka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Kuranko (Koranko) people and territory in northeastern Sierra Leone and Guinea are documented in early modern and 19th-century CE accounts.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and highland territory of the Kuranko people

b_kuranka.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and territorial name of the Mande-speaking Kuranko people inhabiting the highlands of northeastern Sierra Leone and southern Guinea.

b_seradu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Seradu is a modern village in Koinadugu District, Northern Province, Sierra Leone.

morphemes.translation: local village name in Koinadugu District

b_seradu.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in Koinadugu District, northeastern Sierra Leone, lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_mafindi-kabaya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Mafindi-Kabaya is a modern locality in the Kuranko/Koinadugu borderland of Guinea and Sierra Leone.
b_mafindi-kabaya.etymology_analysis: Compound Mande toponym from the Sierra Leone-Guinea highlands, unattested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_nyada.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Nyada is a local toponym in the Kuranko region without pre-867 CE written records.
b_nyada.etymology_analysis: Local West African toponym in the Sierra Leone-Guinea borderlands, unattested by 867 CE.

b_firiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Firiya (Firia), a historical Yalunka Kamara territory in the Guinea–Sierra Leone borderlands associated with the origins of Solimana, is documented in 19th-century oral traditions and colonial accounts.

morphemes.translation: historical Yalunka chiefdom/territory in the Guinea–Sierra Leone borderland

b_firiya.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Yalunka territorial name (Firiya / Firia) in the highlands north of Sierra Leone, recorded in regional oral history as the Kamara Yalunka land where Solimanga Samura settled prior to the rise of the Solimana state.

b_musala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Musala is a local toponym in the Solimana/Yalunka borderlands without pre-867 CE written records.
b_musala.etymology_analysis: Local Mande/Yalunka settlement toponym in the Guinea-Sierra Leone highlands, unattested by 867 CE.

b_solimana.first_mention_attestation: c. 1800 CE (Solimana / Solima emerged as a Yalunka state in northern Sierra Leone and southern Guinea around 1800 CE with its capital at Falaba, documented by British envoy Alexander Gordon Laing in 1822 CE; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE).
b_solimana.etymology_analysis: Yalunka state name (also spelled Solima or Solimane) established in the highlands of northern Sierra Leone and southern Guinea around 1800 CE.

b_limba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Limba people of northern Sierra Leone are documented in external records from the Atlantic slave-trade era (16th-18th centuries CE) onward.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and territory of the Limba people

b_limba.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Limba people, an indigenous group of northern Sierra Leone and adjacent Guinea speaking a distinct Atlantic/Niger-Congo language.

b_siguiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Siguiri, a historic Malinke gold-mining town on the upper Niger River in Guinea, is documented in 19th-century European and French colonial records (with a French military post built in 1888 CE).
b_siguiri.etymology_analysis: From Maninka/Mandinka Sigui-ri ('place of the buffalo'), a prominent Malinke gold-mining town on the upper Niger River in northeastern Guinea adjacent to the Bouré goldfields.
