b_koroussa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; oral tradition dates Kouroussa's founding by the Keita clan of Balato to the late 15th century CE (c. 1470s), and the first European written eyewitness account is by René Caillié in 1827 CE (published 1830 CE).

morphemes.translation: historic Maninka town on the upper Niger River

b_koroussa.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym (also spelled Kurussa) for the capital of the Hamana traditional state on the upper Niger River in northeastern Guinea.

b_balato.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Balato appears in Malinke oral traditions as the first settlement of the Keita migrants from Kita before their move to Kouroussa in the 1470s CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Maninka town in Kouroussa Prefecture

b_balato.etymology_analysis: Malinke settlement toponym in Kouroussa Prefecture, northeastern Guinea, associated with 15th-century CE Keita migration traditions.

b_tinkisso.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Tinkisso River and village in Guinea are documented in 19th- and 20th-century CE geographic and colonial records.

morphemes.translation: major tributary of the upper Niger River in Guinea

b_tinkisso.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 400-km Tinkisso River flowing from the Fouta Djallon highlands to join the Niger River at Siguiri.

b_diakha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bambougou-Diakha on the Bafing River was founded in the 14th-15th centuries CE by Jakhanke (Diakhanké) scholars originally from Diakha in Macina (attested by Ibn Battuta in 1352-1353 CE).

morphemes.translation: sacred scholarly town named after Diakha in Macina

b_diakha.etymology_analysis: Named after Diakha (Dia) in Macina by Soninke-derived Jakhanke Muslim clerics who established Bambougou-Diakha along the Bafing River during the Mali Empire era.

b_dakajalan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dakajalan is known from the 13th-century CE Sunjata oral epic as an early seat/town in the Manden heartland.

morphemes.translation: historic town in the Manden heartland

b_dakajalan.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym (rendered 'Dakadschalan' in German orthography) appearing in the Sunjata oral tradition as an early seat of the Mali Empire.

b_mani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Mani is a local Mande toponym in the Manding heartland without pre-867 CE written records.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Manding region

b_mani.etymology_analysis: Local Mande settlement toponym in the upper Niger / Manding region, unattested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_moribugu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Moribugu is a Mande settlement toponym without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_moribugu.etymology_analysis: From Malinke/Bambara mori ('marabout, Islamic cleric') + bugu ('hamlet, settlement'), meaning 'marabout's village', reflecting post-Islamization Mande settlement naming.

b_kankan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kankan was founded as a caravan center on the Milo River by Soninke/Maninka-mori merchants in the 17th-18th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: historic trading city on the Milo River

b_kankan.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym (Kánkàn) for the major commercial center of Upper Guinea on the Milo River, founded by Maninka-mori clerics and Soninke traders in the 17th-18th centuries CE.

b_jelibakoro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Jelibakoro is a Mande settlement toponym in Upper Guinea without pre-867 CE written records.
b_jelibakoro.etymology_analysis: From Malinke jeli ('griot') + ba ('great') + koro ('old'), a Mande compound settlement name in Upper Guinea.

b_fadama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Fadama is a modern town in Kouroussa Prefecture, Kankan Region, Guinea.
b_fadama.etymology_analysis: Guinean settlement toponym located in Kouroussa Prefecture in the Kankan Region, lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_amana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Hamana (Amana) is documented in Malinke oral tradition as a traditional state formed around Kouroussa in the late 15th century CE (c. 1470s).
b_amana.etymology_analysis: Variant of Hamana, the historic Maninka cultural region and traditional state along the upper Niger River centered on Kouroussa in Guinea.

b_niani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Niani on the Sankarani River in Guinea is traditionally associated with the 13th-14th century CE Mali Empire, though contemporary Arabic writers (al-Umari c. 1340 CE, Ibn Battuta 1352 CE, Ibn Khaldun) refer to the capital simply as 'Mali'.

morphemes.translation: traditional capital of the Mali Empire in eastern Guinea

b_niani.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym for the village on the Sankarani River in eastern Guinea, traditionally identified since the 1920s as the medieval capital of the Mali Empire.

b_figuira.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Figuira (Figuira-Toma) is a modern town in Kangaba Cercle, southwestern Mali.

morphemes.translation: town in Kangaba Cercle, southwestern Mali

b_figuira.etymology_analysis: Malinke settlement toponym in the Kangaba Cercle of southwestern Mali, lacking pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_wasulu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Wassoulou (Wasulu) is documented in 19th-century CE sources, notably as the heartland of Samori Touré's Wassoulou Empire (1878-1898 CE).

morphemes.translation: historical and cultural region straddling southern Mali, Guinea, and Ivory Coast

b_wasulu.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym (Wassoulou, Wasulu) for the Fula-influenced Mande cultural zone in southern Mali and northeastern Guinea, famous for the 19th-century CE Wassoulou Empire.

b_yanfolila.first_mention_attestation: Attested in modern Malian administrative records upon creation of Yanfolila Cercle by Law No. 117 of 11 August 1961 CE; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_yanfolila.etymology_analysis: Yanfolila is a Maninka (Mandé) toponym in the Wassoulou region of southern Mali, traditionally interpreted with the Mandé locative suffix -la ('place of'). It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE and appears in modern administrative records from 1961 CE.

b_kamaro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; no documented contemporary medieval attestation found.
b_kamaro.etymology_analysis: Kamaro is a Mandé toponym in the Upper Niger / Niani area associated with the Maninka Kamara (Camara) clan lineage. It has no confirmed written attestation by 867 CE.

b_sibi_mali.first_mention_attestation: Prominent in the 13th-century CE oral Epic of Sundiata (c. 1235 CE), later recorded in 20th-century transcriptions; unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: borassus palm (rônier) or traditional Mandinka settlement name

b_sibi_mali.etymology_analysis: Siby (Sibi) is a historic Mandinka town southwest of Bamako where, according to the Epic of Sundiata, Sundiata Keita and allied Mandinka warlords gathered before the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235 CE). It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_koulikoro.first_mention_attestation: Documented in late 19th-century CE French colonial expedition accounts (e.g., Gallieni 1880 CE and Binger 1887 CE); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_koulikoro.etymology_analysis: Koulikoro (Bambara: Kulikoro) derives from Bambara kulu ('hill, mountain') and koro ('under, at the foot of'), meaning 'at the foot of the hill', referring to the rocky hills overlooking the Niger River. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_kirina.first_mention_attestation: Famous from the c. 1235 CE Battle of Kirina in Mandinka oral tradition (Epic of Sundiata), recorded in writing in the modern era; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_kirina.etymology_analysis: Kirina (also Krina) is a Mandinka settlement in the Koulikoro Region of Mali, site of Sundiata Keita's decisive c. 1235 CE victory over Sosso king Sumanguru Kanté. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_tabon.first_mention_attestation: Appears in the 13th-century CE oral Epic of Sundiata (Battle of Tabon, c. 1234–1235 CE), recorded in writing in the 20th century CE; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_tabon.etymology_analysis: Tabon is a Mandinka town remembered in the Epic of Sundiata as an early ally of Sundiata Keita and site of a battle against Sosso forces prior to Kirina (c. 1235 CE). It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_kangaba.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the sacred Kamablon sanctuary built in 1653 CE and modern Mandé historical accounts; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_kangaba.etymology_analysis: Kangaba (Kaaba) is a historic Mandinka town in southwestern Mali, home to the Kamablon sacred hut constructed in 1653 CE. While oral tradition links it to the early Keita clan, it has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_konfara.first_mention_attestation: Known from modern geographical gazetteers in Siguiri Prefecture, Guinea, and echoed in the title/epithet Maghan Konfara in the oral Epic of Sundiata; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in Upper Niger Manden

b_konfara.etymology_analysis: Konfara is a Mandé settlement in Siguiri Prefecture, Guinea, near the traditional Manden heartland. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_birnin_lafiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Birnin Lafiya (Birni-Lafia), a town on the Niger River in northern Benin (Karimama Commune, Alibori Department), is documented only in post-medieval and modern administrative records.
b_birnin_lafiya.etymology_analysis: Hausa/Dendi compound toponym (Birni-Lafia / Birnin Lafiya) meaning 'walled city of peace/well-being', incorporating the Arabic loanword lafiya (al-ʿāfiya), situated on the right bank of the Niger River in northern Benin.

b_pekinga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; known only from modern Beninese/Dendi geographical and archaeological records.
b_pekinga.etymology_analysis: Pekinga (Pékinga) is a settlement in northern Benin near the Mékrou–Niger confluence in the Dendi region. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_sota.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern Beninese hydrological and geographical records.
b_sota.etymology_analysis: Sota takes its name from the Sota River, a 250 km tributary of the Niger River in northern Benin's Dendi/Alibori region. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_rozi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Rozi, remembered in Nigerien oral traditions as the last capital of the pre-colonial state of Dyamare in the Dallol Bosso valley of western Niger, is documented only in modern ethnographic and historical reconstructions.

morphemes.translation: traditional capital of Dyamare in the Dallol Bosso

b_rozi.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Dallol Bosso / Niger valley region of western Niger, recorded in regional oral history as a historic seat of the Dyamare polity.

b_dosso.first_mention_attestation: Dosso Kingdom is dated in historical tradition to c. 1750 CE under Zarmakoy Aboubacar, and documented in 19th-century CE colonial records; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_dosso.etymology_analysis: Dosso is a city in southwestern Niger that became the seat of the Zarma Dosso Kingdom around 1750 CE. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_gaya2.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 1895 CE French colonial treaty records and local legends dating settlement to the early 19th century CE; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: riverine trading town on the Niger

b_gaya2.etymology_analysis: Gaya is a river port town on the Niger River in southern Niger (Dosso Region). Local oral tradition places its Songhay founding in the early 19th century CE, with colonial records from 1895 CE; unattested by 867 CE.

b_zarmaganda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Zarmaganda ('land of the Zarma'), a highland plateau region in western Niger north of Niamey, is documented in post-medieval Zarma oral traditions and 19th–20th century colonial accounts.
b_zarmaganda.etymology_analysis: Zarma-Songhai regional choronym meaning 'land of the Zarma' (Zarma + ganda, 'land/country'), designating the dry plateau region in western Niger north of Niamey settled by Zarma migrations from the 16th century onward.

b_zarmatarey.first_mention_attestation: Oral traditions place Zarma settlement in Zarmatarey in the 16th–18th centuries CE; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_zarmatarey.etymology_analysis: Zarmatarey means 'land of the Zarma' in Zarma (Zarma + -tarey), designating the southern Zarma heartland in western Niger. Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_sargan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; key b_sargan corresponds to Sargane in Zarmaganda, Niger.
b_sargan.etymology_analysis: Refers to Sargane in the Zarmaganda region of Niger, which has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_ansongo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern Malian administrative and colonial-era records.

morphemes.translation: Songhay riverine town south of Gao

b_ansongo.etymology_analysis: Ansônge is a German-orthography adaptation of Ansongo, a town on the left bank of the Niger River in the Gao Region of Mali. Although the surrounding area has prehistoric archaeological remains, the town name is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_kamgala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern archaeological surveys of the Bentiya/Ansongo sector (1999 CE).

morphemes.translation: locality near Bentiya in the Ansongo sector

b_kamgala.etymology_analysis: Kamgala is a site/locality near Bentiya (Kukiya) in the Ansongo area of eastern Mali. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_gao.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi in Kitab Surat al-Ard (c. 833 CE, before his death in 846/847 CE) as Kawkaw / al-Kuku, and shortly after by al-Ya'qubi (872 CE).

morphemes.translation: royal capital on the Middle Niger Bend

b_gao.etymology_analysis: Kaukau is a German-orthography rendering of medieval Arabic Kawkaw (Gawgaw), the early name for Gao on the Niger River. It is attested prior to 867 CE in al-Khwarizmi's Kitab Surat al-Ard (c. 833 CE).

b_gadei.first_mention_attestation: Excavated archaeologically as a quarter of Gao Ancien (occupied from the late 1st millennium CE), but the quarter name Gadei/Gadeye is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_gadei.etymology_analysis: Gadei (Gadeye) is one of the historic quarters of Gao, Mali, located along the Niger River. While archaeological layers at Gao date to the first millennium CE, the name Gadei has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sarnah.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by the Egyptian chronicler al-Muhallabi (c. 985 CE, d. 990 CE, preserved in Yaqut), who described Sarnah as the market town of Kawkaw (post-867 CE).

morphemes.translation: market town paired with royal Kawkaw (Gao-Saney)

b_sarnah.etymology_analysis: Sarnah (Sarneh) is the medieval Arabic name recorded by al-Muhallabi (c. 985 CE) for the commercial twin town of Gao, generally identified archaeologically with Gao-Saney. Its written attestation is post-867 CE.

b_koima.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological surface deposits near Koïma predate the 9th century CE, but the toponym Koïma itself is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: village and sand dune (La Dune Rose) opposite Gao

b_koima.etymology_analysis: Koima (Koïma) is a Songhay village on the right bank of the Niger River near Gao, adjacent to the famous pink sand dune (Koïma Hondo / La Dune Rose). The name is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_bourem.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern Malian and colonial-era geographical records.

morphemes.translation: town at the great bend of the Niger River

b_bourem.etymology_analysis: Bourem is a town on the left bank of the Niger River in the Gao Region of northeastern Mali where the river bends sharply. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_kukiya.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly named as Kukiya (Kūkiyā) in the 17th-century CE Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan, 1655 CE, and Tarikh al-Fattash); earlier Arabic writers such as al-Idrisi (1154 CE) mention Kugha, sometimes conflated with Kukiya, both post-867 CE.

morphemes.translation: early Songhay royal and trading center (Bentiya)

b_kukiya.etymology_analysis: Kukîje is a German-orthography rendering of Kukiya (Kukyia), the early Songhay center identified with the archaeological site of Bentiya southeast of Gao. Though central to Songhay oral tradition, it is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_tillaberi.first_mention_attestation: Documented in French colonial administrative records (Tillabéry cercle established 1927 CE); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: market town on the Niger River in western Niger

b_tillaberi.etymology_analysis: Tillaberi (Tillabéri) is a market town and regional capital on the left bank of the Niger River in western Niger. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_tando_husubiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; no contemporary medieval written attestation found.
b_tando_husubiya.etymology_analysis: Tando Husubiya is a Songhay locality name in the Middle Niger / Kukiya sphere. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_tirakka.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (and later al-Idrisi in 1154 CE) as Tirka / Tireqqa, a market center on the Niger Bend (post-867 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval trans-Saharan market town on the Niger Bend

b_tirakka.etymology_analysis: Tirâkke is a German-orthography rendering of medieval Tirakka (Tireqqa), a major Niger Bend market town where merchants from Ghana and Tadmakka met, first documented by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (post-867 CE).

b_kabara.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by Ibn Battuta in 1353 CE as the Niger River port of Timbuktu (post-867 CE).
b_kabara.etymology_analysis: Kabara is the historic Niger River port 8 km south of Timbuktu, first documented in writing by Ibn Battuta in 1353 CE (post-867 CE).

b_timbuktu.first_mention_attestation: 1353 CE (first written mention by Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta, who visited Timbuktu in 1353 CE during his 1352–1353 journey through the Mali Empire; also depicted on the Catalan Atlas of 1375 CE; traditionally founded c. 1100 CE as a seasonal Tuareg camp).

morphemes.translation: small dune / hollow (or legendary caretaker name Buktu in folk etymology)

b_timbuktu.etymology_analysis: Tuareg/Berber toponym (Tin-Buktu / Tombouctou) for the famed caravan and scholarly city near the Niger Bend founded c. 1100 CE; scholarly proposals derive it from Tamasheq tin ('place of') plus buktu ('small dune') or a Zenaga Berber root meaning 'distant/hidden', while the 17th-century Tarikh al-Sudan preserves a folk etymology naming an elderly caretaker woman, Buktu.

b_killi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern locality in the Timbuktu / Inland Niger Delta lacustrine zone.

morphemes.translation: settlement in the Timbuktu lacustrine zone

b_killi.etymology_analysis: Killi is a locality in the lacustrine zone of the Timbuktu region of Mali. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_arawan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; known as a post-medieval Saharan caravan entrepôt north of Timbuktu on the Taoudenni salt route.

morphemes.translation: Saharan caravan oasis north of Timbuktu

b_arawan.etymology_analysis: Arawân is a Germanized spelling of Araouane (Arawan), a Saharan caravan oasis 243 km north of Timbuktu on the route to Taoudenni. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_arawan_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Arawan Road is a modern English geographic descriptor for the trans-Saharan salt-caravan route running north from Timbuktu through the oasis of Araouane (founded in the 16th century CE) toward Taoudenni.

morphemes.translation: Araouane (Saharan caravan oasis north of Timbuktu)

b_arawan_road.etymology_analysis: Modern English descriptive compound referring to the trans-Saharan caravan track connecting Timbuktu to the Saharan oasis of Araouane (Arawan) and the Taoudenni salt mines, attested only from the early modern period onward.

b_sine.first_mention_attestation: c. 1455 CE (first recorded in European written accounts by Venetian navigator Alvise Cadamosto and Portuguese explorers as 'Barbaçim', corrupting the Wolof title Bur-ba-Sine, 'King of Sine'; the Guelowar Kingdom of Sine was established c. 1335–1350 CE).

eponym.details: According to Serer dynastic tradition, the Kingdom of Sine (Siin) was named during the Guelowar era (c. 1350 CE) after Sine-o-Méo Manneh (Siin o Meo Maane), sister of Maysa Wali Manneh, the first Guelowar king of Sine.

morphemes.translation: Sine (historic Serer kingdom in west-central Senegal)

b_sine.etymology_analysis: From Serer Siin (French/English Sine), a pre-colonial Serer kingdom in Senegal established under the Guelowar dynasty c. 1350 CE and traditionally named after Sine-o-Méo Manneh (sister of Maysa Wali Manneh); first recorded in European sources in the mid-15th century as Barbaçim (from Wolof Bur-ba-Sine).

b_laa_baol.first_mention_attestation: Known from oral traditions of the Kingdom of Baol (16th–19th centuries CE) as a province ruled by the Beersin Laa; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_laa_baol.etymology_analysis: Laa was a historic province of the Kingdom of Baol in Senegal, governed by a lamane bearing the title Beersin Laa. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_lambaye.first_mention_attestation: Served as the capital of the Kingdom of Baol (traditionally 11th–19th centuries CE, with archaeological and historical records from c. 1400–1900 CE); unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: royal capital of the Kingdom of Baol

b_lambaye.etymology_analysis: Lambaye is a historic town in central Senegal that served as the royal capital (seat of the Teigne) of the Kingdom of Baol. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_mbul.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the new capital of Cayor by Amary Ngone Sobel Fall following the Battle of Danki in 1549 CE; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: royal capital of the Kingdom of Cayor

b_mbul.etymology_analysis: Embûl is a Germanized spelling of Mboul (Mbul), founded as the centrally located capital of the Kingdom of Cayor in 1549 CE after the Battle of Danki. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_waalo.first_mention_attestation: Associated in oral and written historiography with the founding of the Kingdom of Waalo by Ndiadiane Ndiaye c. 1287 CE, and documented by Europeans from the 15th century CE; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_waalo.etymology_analysis: Waalo (Walo) is a Wolof geographical term denoting seasonally inundated floodplain agricultural land along the lower Senegal River, which gave its name to the Kingdom of Waalo (traditionally founded c. 1287 CE). Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_yoff.first_mention_attestation: Historically recorded as founded in 1432 CE as the Lebou fishing village of Mbohehe; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Lebou coastal settlement on the Cap-Vert peninsula

b_yoff.etymology_analysis: Yoff (Wolof: Yoof) is a historic Lebou fishing town on the northern shore of Dakar's Cap-Vert peninsula, founded in 1432 CE. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_ouarak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; key b_ouarak corresponds to Ouarak in Louga Region, Senegal.
b_ouarak.etymology_analysis: Refers to Ouarak (Pété Ouarak) in the Louga Region of Senegal, unattested by 867 CE.

b_bakel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Bakel, a Soninke trading town on the left bank of the upper Senegal River in eastern Senegal, is documented in early modern and 19th-century European trade records (French Fort Bakel was constructed in 1818 CE and visited by René Caillié in 1819 CE).

morphemes.translation: trading town on the left bank of the upper Senegal River

b_bakel.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Soninke town name on the upper Senegal River in eastern Senegal within the historic Kingdom of Gajaaga (Galam), which became a major gum-arabic trading post and site of French Fort Bakel (built 1818 CE).

b_arondo.first_mention_attestation: Excavated as a late 1st- and early 2nd-millennium CE Iron Age archaeological site at the Senegal–Falémé confluence, but the toponym Arondo is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: settlement at the Senegal–Falémé river confluence

b_arondo.etymology_analysis: Arondo is a village and Iron Age archaeological site at the confluence of the Senegal and Falémé rivers in eastern Senegal (Gajaaga). The name is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_galam.first_mention_attestation: c. 1650 CE (the Soninke kingdom of Gajaaga, known by the Wolof exonym Galam, existed from before 1000 CE in oral tradition and was documented by European traders from the 17th century CE; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE).

morphemes.translation: gold (exonym for the Soninke kingdom and region of Gajaaga)

b_galam.etymology_analysis: Wolof exonym (meaning 'gold') applied to the historic Soninke kingdom and region of Gajaaga along the upper Senegal River, documented in European sources from the 17th century CE.

b_jowol.first_mention_attestation: Known from Futa Toro oral traditions and modern Mauritanian records as Djowol; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic town on the Senegal River in Futa Toro

b_jowol.etymology_analysis: Dschowôl is a German-orthography rendering of Jowol (Djowol / Diowol), an ancient town on the Senegal River in southern Mauritania. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_wompu.first_mention_attestation: Known from Soninke oral traditions of the historic Haïré province and modern Mauritanian records (commune established 1987 CE); unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Soninke village of the Haïré province

b_wompu.etymology_analysis: Wompu (Wompou) is a town in the Guidimakha Region of southern Mauritania on the Senegal River, historically part of the Soninke province of Haïré. It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_ngoppugu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; no contemporary medieval written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Middle Senegal Valley

b_ngoppugu.etymology_analysis: Ngoppugu is a local toponym in the Middle Senegal Valley (Jowol/Silla area). It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_silla.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by al-Bakri in 1068 CE as Silla (Sīlā), a major kingdom and town on the Senegal River (post-867 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval trading kingdom on the Senegal River

b_silla.etymology_analysis: Sîlle is a Germanized spelling of Silla (Sīlā), an important Islamicized trading town and kingdom on the Senegal River first attested in writing by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (post-867 CE).

b_ogo.first_mention_attestation: Excavated as a protohistoric iron-working site in the Matam region and linked in Futa Toro oral tradition to the Dia-Ogo dynasty, but unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_ogo.etymology_analysis: Ogo is a village and protohistoric metallurgical archaeological site in the Matam Region of Senegal, associated in Futa Toro oral tradition with the early Dia-Ogo dynasty. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_cubalel.first_mention_attestation: Excavated archaeologically as a 1st-millennium CE settlement mound complex in the Middle Senegal Valley, but the name Cubalel is unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: archaeological mound complex in the Middle Senegal Valley

b_cubalel.etymology_analysis: Cubalel is a major archaeological mound site in the Middle Senegal Valley studied for first-millennium CE Takrur settlement and ironworking. The modern site name is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_dhraina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; no contemporary medieval written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: settlement in southern Mauritania / Lower Senegal Valley

b_dhraina.etymology_analysis: Draîne is a Germanized spelling of Dhraina, a locality in the Lower Senegal / Trarza borderlands. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_anate.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; no contemporary medieval written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local toponym in the Takrur sphere

b_anate.etymology_analysis: Anate is a local toponym in the Lower Senegal / Takrur region. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_podor.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 18th-century CE French colonial records (Fort de Podor established in the 1740s CE); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: river town on Île à Morfil

b_podor.etymology_analysis: Podôr is a Germanized spelling of Podor, a historic town on Île à Morfil in the Senegal River valley that became a French trading post in the 18th century CE. Unattested by 867 CE.

b_dagana.first_mention_attestation: Local tradition places the village's founding in the 14th century CE, with contemporary written documentation from 1820 CE when the French built a fort; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

morphemes.translation: settlement on the lower Senegal River

b_dagana.etymology_analysis: Dagana is a town on the left bank of the Senegal River in northern Senegal, traditionally founded in the 14th century CE and documented from 1820 CE. Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_takrur.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources by al-Bakri in 1068 CE as Takrūr (describing its early 11th-century CE ruler War Jabi and its Muslim population); post-867 CE.

morphemes.translation: medieval state and capital in the Middle Senegal Valley

b_takrur.etymology_analysis: Takrûr is a Germanized spelling of Takrur (Tekrur), the medieval state on the Senegal River first attested in written Arabic sources by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (post-867 CE).

b_waram.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the late 8th-century CE geographical list of Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Fazari (c. 772–790 CE, cited in Pingree 1970 and later Arabic geographers) as a Lower Senegal Valley polity called Waram.
b_waram.etymology_analysis: Waram is attested in the late 8th-century CE work of the astronomer-geographer al-Fazari as a densely populated polity in the Lower Senegal Valley, making it one of the earliest documented names in Senegambia prior to 867 CE.

b_awlil.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in the late 10th century CE by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977–988 CE) and later by al-Bakri (1068 CE) as the coastal salt-producing island/locality of Awlīl (post-867 CE).

morphemes.translation: coastal salt-pan entrepôt near the Senegal River mouth

b_awlil.etymology_analysis: Awlîl is a Germanized spelling of Awlil (Aulil), the famous coastal salt-producing center near the mouth of the Senegal River attested from the late 10th century CE (Ibn Hawqal 977 CE, al-Bakri 1068 CE), post-867 CE.

b_tyeng.first_mention_attestation: Remembered in Wolof oral tradition as the initial capital of the Jolof Empire (c. 1350–1360 CE); unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: early capital of the Jolof Empire

b_tyeng.etymology_analysis: Tjênch is a German-orthography rendering of Thieng (Tyeng), the initial capital of the Jolof Empire in Wolof oral tradition (c. 14th century CE) before the seat moved to Yang-Yang. Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_danki.first_mention_attestation: Associated with the decisive Battle of Danki in 1549 CE between Cayor and the Jolof Empire; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: site of the 1549 CE Battle of Danki in Senegal

b_danki.etymology_analysis: Danki is the site near a lake in Senegal where Amary Ngone Sobel Fall defeated the Buurba Jolof in 1549 CE, triggering the breakup of the Jolof Empire. Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_mboynane.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern village in the Louga Region of Senegal.

morphemes.translation: village in the Jolof / Louga region

b_mboynane.etymology_analysis: Mboynane is a settlement in the Louga Region (historic Jolof) of Senegal. It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_namandirou.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 16th-century CE Portuguese accounts (André Donelha, describing events c. 1460 CE) and Wolof/Fula oral traditions; unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_namandirou.etymology_analysis: Namandirû is a Germanized spelling of Namandirou (also known as Njarmeew), a historic kingdom in eastern Senegal whose name means 'country of abundance'. Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

b_mboune.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern settlement in the Louga / Ferlo region of Senegal.
b_mboune.etymology_analysis: Mboune is a settlement in central-northern Senegal (Namandirou/Jolof area). It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_linguere.first_mention_attestation: Linguère is documented in modern Senegalese history (named after the Wolof/Serer royal title Lingeer); unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_linguere.etymology_analysis: Linguere (Linguère) is a town in the Louga Region of Senegal (historic Jolof), sharing its name with the Wolof/Serer royal title Lingeer ('queen' or 'princess'). It is unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
